name: Risk-Adjusted QS Returns
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Pricing the Difference Between a Product and a Promise
lesson.summary: Because quantum sensing already generates revenue and needs far less unproven hardware than fault-tolerant quantum computing, it carries a fundamentally different, generally lower, risk-adjusted return profile, even though its ceiling is smaller.
lesson.body:
Risk-adjusted return, as introduced earlier, asks not just how large a potential payoff is, but how large it is relative to the uncertainty of actually collecting it. Two investments can have the same expected value on paper and still be very different bets, if one of them has a tight, well understood range of outcomes and the other has a wide range that includes both spectacular success and total loss. Quantum computing and quantum sensing, despite sharing the word quantum and often the same corporate parent, sit at very different points on that risk spectrum, for reasons the last few chapters have laid out directly.

A company betting its future on fault-tolerant, general purpose quantum computing is making a bet with a genuinely uncertain technical outcome. It needs the million qubit scale error correction problem to be solved, on a timeline nobody can currently specify with confidence, using an architecture that has not been settled among competing approaches such as superconducting circuits, trapped ions, and photonics. If it works, the payoff could be enormous, because a working fault-tolerant quantum computer would have applications across cryptography, chemistry, and optimization that no other technology can match. If it does not work on the timeline investors are pricing in, or a rival architecture wins the race, the payoff could be close to zero. That is a binary, long horizon bet, and its risk-adjusted return is difficult to estimate honestly because so much of the technical uncertainty has not yet been resolved by real world demonstration.

A company focused on quantum sensing is making a narrower but much better characterized bet. The underlying physics already works, the products already ship, and the open questions are the ordinary ones of any hardware business: can it manufacture reliably at lower cost, can it win contracts against competitors, can it expand from a research and defense customer base into broader commercial markets like medical imaging or infrastructure inspection. Those are real risks, and quantum sensing companies can absolutely fail for ordinary business reasons, but they are risks of degree rather than risks of kind. The question is not whether the technology can exist, it already does, but how large and how fast its addressable market grows.

Consider, purely as an illustration and not as investment advice, two hypothetical companies. Company A has raised money against the promise of a future fault-tolerant quantum computer years away, with revenue today coming mostly from cloud access to small, error prone research devices and from services contracts, while its investment case depends on believing the roadmap to error correction at scale. Company B sells quantum gravimeters to mining and infrastructure firms today, has recurring survey and hardware revenue, and its investment case depends on believing that market keeps growing and that it can defend its share of it. Company A's outcomes are more spread out, a bigger possible upside but a real possibility of near total loss if the technical roadmap stalls. Company B's outcomes are more clustered, a smaller plausible upside but a much lower chance of the underlying technology simply failing to work, because it already has. Neither is automatically the better investment, that depends on an investor's time horizon and risk tolerance, but conflating the two, treating them as the same kind of bet because both say quantum on the label, is the exact error this book has been trying to train a skeptical reader to avoid.
